strengths: The paper targets an important and under-addressed practical failure mode in object removal: removing associated effects such as shadows and reflections while preserving the rest of the image. This is a meaningful computer vision contribution beyond standard masked inpainting.

The OBER dataset is a useful contribution. It includes paired camera-captured data, simulated composites, object masks, object-effect masks, and multi-object cases. The explicit annotation of object/effect regions is valuable and supports supervision and evaluation that prior datasets often lack.

The proposed Object-Effect Attention and attention-guided fusion are simple but well-motivated. Supervising cross-attention with object-effect masks gives the model a mechanism to localize effects beyond the input object mask, and the fusion strategy directly addresses background drift from diffusion/VAE reconstruction.

The empirical results are strong on the reported benchmarks. ObjectClear substantially improves PSNR, PSNR-BG, LPIPS, and CLIP distance on OBER-Test and RORD-Val, and performs competitively on OBER-Wild using the reference-free ReMOVE metric. The ablations support the contribution of mask supervision, simulated data, and especially attention-guided fusion.

Qualitative examples are convincing and show challenging cases with shadows, reflections, and mutually occluding objects. The appendix adds useful evidence including user-study results, robustness to coarse strokes, and limitations.
weaknesses: The novelty of the method is moderate. Attention supervision over masks and final image fusion/copy-paste using a predicted soft mask are natural extensions of existing diffusion editing and localized attention ideas. The dataset is arguably the stronger contribution than the model architecture.

The fairness and scope of the comparisons need care. ObjectClear is trained on the newly curated OBER data with object-effect supervision, while most baselines are not adapted to this dataset/task. The paper does evaluate baselines with object-effect masks, but this does not fully isolate the benefit of the model design from the benefit of task-specific data.

The OBER-Test set is small, with only 160 camera-captured test pairs, and OBER-Wild lacks ground truth. The main quantitative gains are therefore partly established on a limited in-domain test set and a reference-free metric whose reliability for object-effect removal is not deeply analyzed.

The object-effect mask generation and alpha compositing pipeline has technical ambiguities. Difference-threshold masks may capture camera noise, lighting changes, or misalignment, and the alpha formula for effect regions is only briefly specified despite being central to the simulated data quality. More validation of mask accuracy and compositing realism would strengthen the dataset claim.

The large jump from ablation setting (c) to (d) suggests that attention-guided fusion heavily drives the reported fidelity metrics, especially PSNR-BG. This is useful for preserving background, but the paper should more thoroughly analyze failure cases where the predicted attention mask misses long or overlapping effects, since fusion would then preserve residual shadows/reflections.

Claims about object insertion and movement are under-evaluated. They are presented as additional applications, but the evidence is mostly qualitative and does not carry the same experimental support as object removal.

Reproducibility details are incomplete for dataset construction and evaluation. The paper gives training settings, but manual annotation protocols, threshold choices, shadow-direction grouping, reflection-pair selection, and exact evaluation splits would need to be released or specified more precisely for faithful reproduction.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical limitation of object removal: removing shadows/reflections and preserving the unedited background, rather than only filling the object mask.

The proposed OBER dataset, if released as described, would be useful: it includes paired counterfactual captures, object masks, object-effect masks, simulated composites, multi-object cases, and separate test/wild sets.

The method is simple and plausible: conditioning SDXL-Inpainting on the original image plus object crop, supervising object-effect attention, and using the resulting attention map for fusion directly addresses the stated failure mode.

The quantitative results are consistently strong across reported metrics, especially on OBER-Test, and the ablations show each component improving performance, with a large gain from attention-guided fusion.
The paper includes comparisons to many recent inpainting/object-removal baselines and discusses limitations involving overlapping or very large shadows.
weaknesses: The empirical case is weakened by evaluation design. The largest gains come from attention-guided fusion, but the paper does not apply comparable background-copy/fusion postprocessing to baselines using the provided object-effect masks. This makes the background-fidelity comparison potentially unfair, especially for PSNR-BG.

The strongest benchmark, OBER-Test, is only 160 samples and comes from the authors' own capture pipeline. OBER-Wild has no ground truth and is evaluated mainly with ReMOVE, so the evidence for broad real-world generalization is limited.

The dataset construction is under-specified and technically questionable in places. The alpha-map equation for effects is unclear for color images, reflections, and non-black shadows, and the text appears to contain a set-operation error for the background area. The simulated data quality and manual filtering criteria are not rigorously validated.

The paper's novelty is moderate. The core model is SDXL-Inpainting with stacked visual/text conditioning, attention supervision, and mask-based blending; these are reasonable combinations of existing ideas rather than a clearly new modeling principle.

The ablation table shows only aggregate performance on one setting and does not isolate key confounders, such as original-image input versus masked-image input, learned attention versus ground-truth/object-effect-mask fusion, or whether the attention loss mainly helps by producing a better blending mask.

Reproducibility details are incomplete for a CVPR-level dataset/method paper: there is no clear statement of dataset release, licensing for downloaded Internet backgrounds, annotation protocol, threshold choices for difference masks, or variance over random seeds/splits.

Some claims are overstated relative to the evidence. The paper repeatedly says ObjectClear outperforms methods even with object-effect masks, but without equalizing fusion/postprocessing and with limited external ground-truth testing, this conclusion is not fully supported.

Presentation has several errors and inconsistencies, including swapped citations in Table 1 rows, typos such as Object-Affect Attention, and ambiguous terminology around object mask, effect mask, and object-effect mask. These are presentation issues, but they also make some experimental details harder to trust.

strengths: The paper targets an important and practical failure mode in object removal: removing object-induced effects such as shadows and reflections while preserving the untouched background. This is a meaningful problem beyond generic inpainting, and the framing is well motivated with clear qualitative examples.

The proposed OBER dataset is a strong contribution. It combines 2,715 camera-captured pairs with 10,000 simulated samples, provides object and object-effect masks, includes shadows/reflections and multi-object cases, and adds OBER-Test and OBER-Wild benchmarks. This would likely be useful to the community if released.

ObjectClear is technically sensible: feeding the original image rather than a masked image, supervising object-effect cross-attention with foreground masks, and using the predicted attention for fusion all directly address the stated problem. The attention-guided fusion is especially practical for preserving background detail.

The empirical results are strong across multiple datasets and metrics. On OBER-Test, ObjectClear substantially improves PSNR, PSNR-BG, LPIPS, and CLIP distance over open-source baselines, and it remains competitive or better even when baselines are given object-effect masks. The RORD-Val and OBER-Wild results also support the claims.

The ablation study is useful and supports the main design choices: Lmask, simulated data, and attention-guided fusion each improve results, with AG fusion producing a large gain in background preservation. The supplementary user study and stroke-mask examples further strengthen the practical case.

The manuscript is generally clear, well organized, and visually convincing. The method, dataset pipeline, and comparisons are easy to follow, and the limitations section honestly identifies difficult cases such as overlapping or very large shadows.
weaknesses: The model-side novelty is moderate. The core architecture builds on SDXL-Inpainting, CLIP embeddings, cross-attention supervision, and copy-paste/fusion ideas that are related to prior personalization and inpainting/editing methods. The paper’s strongest contribution is arguably the dataset and task formulation rather than a fundamentally new modeling approach.

Some dataset construction details are under-specified or technically ambiguous. The pixel-difference threshold for object-effect masks, manual correction protocol, alpha clipping/normalization, treatment of color channels, Gaussian blur parameters, and object-aware dilation/erosion rules are not fully specified. Eq. 1 for alpha estimation is also unclear: the condition for background uses Mo ∩ Me, and the ratio (Igt - Iin)/(Igt + eps) can be negative or channel-dependent depending on the effect type.

The evaluation depends heavily on the new OBER data, but the OBER-Test split is small at 160 samples. More detail is needed on whether train/test share object instances, scenes, lighting setups, or extracted foreground assets, since such overlap could inflate results on the proposed benchmark.

Baseline fairness is mostly addressed by evaluating both object-only and object-effect masks, but baselines are not fine-tuned on OBER, while ObjectClear is. This is reasonable for comparing off-the-shelf tools, but it does not isolate whether the gains come from the dataset, architecture, or training distribution. Fine-tuning at least the closest open-source baseline on OBER would make the evidence stronger.

The OBER-Wild evaluation uses ReMOVE as the sole quantitative metric because no ground truth exists. This provides some signal, but reference-free erasure metrics are imperfect and can miss semantic artifacts or over-smoothing. The user study helps, but more details on sampling, randomization, interface, and statistical significance would improve confidence.

The very large ablation jump from AG fusion suggests that much of the quantitative gain comes from copying the original background outside the predicted attention region. This is useful, but it also makes performance sensitive to attention-mask quality; failure cases where AG fusion preserves residual effects or blends incorrectly are not analyzed quantitatively.

Reproducibility is only partial from the manuscript. Training hyperparameters are given, but implementation details for data generation, annotation, baseline inference settings, prompts, mask preprocessing, attention-map extraction layer choice, and fusion thresholds are insufficient for independent replication without released code and data.

strengths: The paper targets an important and under-addressed failure mode in object removal: removing associated effects such as shadows and reflections while preserving the rest of the image. This is a meaningful practical problem beyond standard masked inpainting.

The OBER dataset is a substantial contribution: paired camera-captured data, simulated composites, object masks, object-effect masks, RGBA foregrounds, and separate OBER-Test/OBER-Wild benchmarks. The annotation types are well matched to the proposed training signal and could be useful to the community if released.

The method is technically plausible and well integrated with SDXL-Inpainting. Adaptive Target-Aware Attention uses visual object embeddings plus mask-supervised attention to localize object-effect regions, while Attention-Guided Fusion and spatially varying denoising directly address common diffusion editing artifacts.

The empirical evidence is broad. The paper compares against many recent inpainting and object-removal baselines on RORD-Val, OBER-Test, OBER-Wild, OmniPaint-Bench, OmniEraser-Bench, and MULAN, and reports consistent gains across PSNR, LPIPS, CLIP/DINO distances, ReMOVE†, qualitative results, and a user study.

The ablations are informative: ATA, simulated data, AGF, and SVDS each improve performance, with AGF/SVDS giving especially large background-fidelity gains. The additional experiment giving baselines ground-truth object-effect masks for blending is a useful attempt to test whether the gains are merely due to background copy-back.
weaknesses: The method contribution is somewhat incremental relative to the dataset contribution. It combines known ingredients, including SDXL fine-tuning, CLIP visual prompting, attention supervision, background fusion, and denoising-strength tuning. The novelty is useful but not conceptually deep.

The evaluation does not fully isolate the effect of the proposed architecture from the new training data. Most baselines appear to be used as available systems rather than retrained or fine-tuned on OBER with comparable data, so the large margins may partly reflect dataset advantage rather than model design. A stronger comparison would include SDXL/BrushNet-like baselines trained on the same OBER data without ATA/AGF/SVDS under matched settings.

OBER-Test is small with only 163 paired test examples and comes from the same capture pipeline as the training set. OBER-Wild is larger but lacks ground truth and uses a modified ReMOVE† metric introduced by the authors, so the most realistic benchmark has weaker objective validation.

Some dataset construction details are under-specified or potentially fragile. The object-effect mask is derived by thresholding pixel differences in before/after captures, which can include alignment, illumination, or camera noise; the paper does not report quality-control statistics or inter-annotator/annotation accuracy. The alpha-map equation and handling of RGB shadows/reflections are also not fully clear.

Reproducibility is only moderate. Training hardware, batch size, learning rate, resolution, and denoising steps are provided, but the manuscript contains placeholder-style links for the dataset/demo, does not clearly commit to code/model release, and omits enough implementation details for exact reproduction of baseline settings, threshold choices, object-effect mask generation, and AGF/SVDS schedules.

The approach inherits limitations of attention-based effect attribution. The paper acknowledges failures with overlapping/intertwined effects, and this is material for real scenes where shadows from multiple objects interact. The current formulation may over-remove non-target effects or under-remove target effects when causal attribution is ambiguous.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical failure mode in object removal: removing associated effects such as shadows and reflections while preserving the rest of the image. This is a meaningful computer vision problem with clear application value.

The proposed OBER dataset is potentially useful. It includes paired images, object masks, object-effect masks, RGBA foregrounds, camera-captured data, simulated data, and explicit reflection/shadow cases, which could support future work if released as promised.

The manuscript evaluates against many recent baselines and reports improvements on RORD-Val, OBER-Test, OBER-Wild, OmniPaint-Bench, OmniEraser-Bench, and a filtered MULAN subset. The quantitative gains on OBER-Test and RORD-Val are large, especially for PSNR-BG and LPIPS.

The ablation table is helpful and shows the relative impact of the proposed components. In particular, Attention-Guided Fusion substantially improves background preservation, and SVDS gives a smaller but consistent additional gain.

The qualitative examples and limitation discussion are generally aligned with the stated task, and the paper clearly identifies difficult cases involving overlapping or interacting shadows/reflections.
weaknesses: The main technical novelty is limited. The method is built on SDXL-Inpainting, adds CLIP object embeddings to cross-attention, supervises attention maps with object-effect masks, and then blends the generated output with the original image. These are reasonable engineering choices, but the conceptual contribution beyond existing attention-guided editing, mask supervision, and copy-back fusion is modest.

A large fraction of the reported gain appears to come from Attention-Guided Fusion rather than the proposed attention mechanism itself. In Table 2, ATA improves PSNR only from 27.29 to 27.56, while AGF raises it from 28.04 to 32.77. This suggests the main performance driver is copying unchanged regions from the input using a predicted mask, which is valuable but less compelling as a core model contribution.

The evaluation metrics strongly favor the proposed fusion strategy. PSNR, PSNR-BG, LPIPS, and CLIP distance on paired fixed-camera data reward preserving the original background exactly, and AGF is explicitly designed to paste the input background back. This makes it difficult to separate genuine object-effect removal quality from metric alignment with the post-processing step.

The fairness of comparisons is not fully convincing. ObjectClear is trained on the new OBER data with object-effect supervision, while most baselines are used as existing pretrained systems and do not have access to comparable training data or a learned object-effect mask predictor. The paper includes a blending-with-ground-truth-mask experiment, but this still does not control for training data, supervision, or architecture adaptation.

The dataset construction has unresolved technical ambiguities. The alpha-map equation is unclear, including the condition for pixels in Mo ∩ Me and how RGB channel differences are converted into alpha. Thresholds for difference-based object-effect masks, alignment quality, manual annotation protocol, and quality control are insufficiently specified for reproducibility.

The simulated and reflection data may introduce selection bias. The appendix states that the authors run their trained model on 200 reflection images and manually select 50 high-quality results to add to training. This self-training/curation loop is not carefully analyzed and may overstate generalization to reflection cases.

The OBER-Test set is small, with only 163 paired examples, and comes from the same capture/data pipeline as the training data. The strongest reported gains are therefore partly on an in-distribution benchmark. External benchmark results are useful but mostly relegated to the appendix and still do not fully address training-data advantage.

The proposed ReMOVE† metric for OBER-Wild is modified from prior work but not validated. Since OBER-Wild lacks ground truth, the claim of superior wild performance rests on a custom metric plus qualitative examples and a small user study.

The user study lacks important details such as randomization, blinding, statistical significance, inter-rater agreement, and whether participants saw method identities or mask settings. The reported preferences are therefore supportive but not strong evidence.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper gives high-level training settings, but many crucial details are missing: exact dataset release status, preprocessing thresholds, attention-map layer/token aggregation, blur parameters, SVDS implementation details, mask augmentations, baseline inference settings, and code/model availability. Several placeholders such as dataset/demo links are not concrete in the manuscript.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practically relevant gap in object removal: removing associated effects such as shadows and reflections while preserving the rest of the image. This is a clear computer vision problem with immediate usefulness for image editing.

The proposed OBER dataset is a meaningful contribution. It includes paired object-present/object-absent images, object masks, object-effect masks, RGBA foregrounds, simulated composites, multi-object cases, and reflection examples. If released as claimed, it would likely be useful beyond this specific method.

The method is well matched to the task. Adaptive Target-Aware Attention uses object/effect mask supervision to learn attention over removal regions, while Attention-Guided Fusion and spatially varying denoising directly target common diffusion inpainting failures: background drift, incomplete removal, and color inconsistency.

The experimental evidence is broad and generally convincing. The paper compares against many recent inpainting and object-removal baselines, evaluates both object-mask and object-effect-mask settings, reports results on RORD-Val, OBER-Test, OBER-Wild, OmniPaint-Bench, OmniEraser-Bench, and MULAN, and includes qualitative comparisons, ablations, and a user study.

The ablation study is strong enough to support the main design choices. ATA, simulated data, AGF, and SVDS each improve the metrics, with AGF especially improving background preservation. Additional experiments with ground-truth object-effect masks for baseline blending help address a likely fairness concern.
The paper is mostly clear and visually well supported. Figures communicate the practical failure modes of prior methods and the intended advantage of the proposed approach.
weaknesses: The novelty of the model is moderate rather than fundamental. The system combines known ingredients around an SDXL inpainting backbone: CLIP visual/text conditioning, attention supervision, output-input fusion, and spatially varying denoising. The dataset and task framing are stronger contributions than the architectural novelty.

The reported gains rely heavily on Attention-Guided Fusion, which copies much of the original background back into the output. This is appropriate for the task, but it also strongly favors metrics such as PSNR-BG and can obscure whether the generative model itself reconstructs better content. The additional blending comparison helps, but the dependence on a good predicted effect mask remains central.

Dataset construction details are not fully reproducible. Important choices such as difference thresholds for object-effect masks, capture protocol, filtering criteria, manual annotation burden, foreground alpha estimation details, background image sources/licensing, and the exact train/test split construction are underspecified.

OBER-Test is relatively small at 163 paired examples, and OBER-Wild lacks ground truth. Since the method is trained on OBER, the strongest in-domain quantitative results may overstate generalization. The additional external benchmarks reduce this concern, but more analysis of distribution overlap and failure cases would strengthen the claim.

The modified ReMOVE† metric for OBER-Wild is introduced without enough validation. It is unclear how well it correlates with human judgments or whether it systematically rewards background copying/fusion strategies.

Fairness of baseline comparisons could be clearer. Methods are run at their default input sizes in some supplemental comparisons, and some baselines receive object-effect masks while others do not. The paper makes efforts to address this, but exact prompt settings, inference steps, resolution handling, and tuning protocol for each baseline should be more transparent.

The paper promises public release of OBER and provides an online demo, but reproducibility still depends on actual release of data, code, trained weights, and implementation details. As written, the work is not fully reproducible from the manuscript alone.

Some technical descriptions are ambiguous or possibly inconsistent, such as the alpha map equation and the handling of overlapping object/effect masks. These do not undermine the main empirical result, but they should be corrected for clarity.

The limitations section is honest but narrow. Complex lighting and overlapping effects are discussed, but other relevant risks such as transparent objects, thin structures, inaccurate user masks, highly reflective surfaces, and semantic hallucination are not evaluated systematically.
